The within-country comparisons show three consistent patterns. First, school bans reduce in-school phone use, though compliance is far from complete: daily smartphone use at school is 12.1 percentage points lower in ban schools (from an overall mean of 55.3%, meaning roughly 43% of students in ban schools still use a phone daily), leisure digital use of more than an hour per day at school falls by 3.7 points, and after-school leisure screen use (\>3 hours/day) is nearly unchanged (−0.8 pp)—a useful check that ban schools are not simply attended by students who avoid screens outside school. Second, students in ban schools report less classroom distraction by digital devices (−3.5 pp overall; −4.2 pp for girls and −2.8 pp for boys). Third, well-being differences are small, favorable, and concentrated among girls: girls in ban schools are 2.0 pp less likely to feel nervous or anxious without their device, 1.4 pp less likely to report feeling lonely at school (versus +0.3 pp for boys), and score +0.02 to +0.03 SD higher on school belonging and life satisfaction. Because this is a cross-sectional comparison across schools, however, it cannot separate the causal effect of a phone ban from unobserved differences in school leadership or student composition.

**Assessment.** Across 80 education systems in PISA 2022, school phone prohibitions are associated with lower in-school phone use, less classroom digital distraction, and slightly lower loneliness and device anxiety among girls. While cross-sectional school comparisons cannot rule out selection into bans, the girl-specific pattern aligns with the quasi-experimental evidence from Norway's middle-school bans and underscores the value of evaluating the 2024–26 U.S. state phone bans as post-ban YRBS and state-survey waves become available.

<a id="review-reconcile"></a>

## How this sits with Haidt's and Twenge's evidence

The [Anxious Generation research pages](https://www.jonathanhaidt.com/articles) and [collaborative reviews](https://www.anxiousgeneration.com/research/collaborative-review-docs) compile a large body of evidence linking smartphones and social media to adolescent distress. Much of the descriptive case comes from Jean Twenge's work with the Monitoring the Future, YRBS, and Millennium Cohort surveys (correlating screen time with depressive symptoms and tracking national trends), paired with natural experiments on broadband and early social-media rollouts. Placing that literature alongside our pilot results clarifies what the public microdata can and cannot confirm: the individual-level association between heavy phone use and distress replicates readily in new settings, but population-level timing tests in public data show no effect, and most of the published causal studies test earlier technologies rather than the post-2010 smartphone transition.

<a id="review-what-that-evidence-base-contains"></a>

### What that evidence base contains

| Evidence type                                                    | Design                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Typical result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cross-sectional use–symptom associations (Twenge and colleagues) | Heavy vs. light users in national surveys (MTF, YRBS, Millennium Cohort, UK and U.S. panels)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Heavy users are roughly twice as likely to report depression or low well-being (adjusted odds ratios 1.7–3.0), with stronger associations among girls                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Longitudinal panels                                              | Screen or social-media use at wave *t* predicting symptoms at *t* + 1                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Small effects; the main point of methodological debate with Orben, Przybylski, Odgers, and Ferguson                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Experiments                                                      | Short-term deactivation and abstinence trials, mostly among college students and adults                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Modest improvements of a few hundredths to roughly 0.2 SD                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Natural experiments                                              | [Facebook college rollout (2004–06)](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faer.20211218); four broadband instrumental-variable studies (Germany, [Italy](https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3949645), Spain, UK) reviewed by [McClean, Rausch, and Haidt](https://ssrn.com/abstract=5188105); and Elaine Guo's [British Columbia study](http://hdl.handle.net/1807/130332) (University of Toronto dissertation, 2023; job-market paper, 2022) linking twenty years of provincial school records to wireless-coverage maps | Facebook arrival: ~0.1 SD worse on a mental-health index, larger for women and higher-risk students. Italy: first DSL access (2001–2013), instrumented by distance to telephone exchanges, raised diagnosed disorders in cohorts exposed before age 20 by 0.08 SD. British Columbia: girls in mountain communities covered by high-speed fixed wireless gained ~1 pp in severe mental-health designations relative to boys from 2014 onward (~90% of baseline), with moderate designations and other disabilities unchanged |
| Aggregate timing                                                 | The [mood-disorders review](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1diMvsMeRphUH7E6D1d_J7R6WbDdgnzFHDHPx9HXzR5o/edit) and the [World Happiness Report chapter](https://www.worldhappiness.report/ed/2026/social-media-is-harming-adolescents-at-a-scale-large-enough-to-cause-changes-at-the-population-level/)                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Flat trends through the Great Recession, an inflection around 2012 led by girls across the Anglosphere and Western Europe, and declining PISA life satisfaction in 40 of 47 countries between 2015 and 2018                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

<a id="review-where-the-pilot-agrees"></a>

### Where the pilot agrees

- In the 2022–23 GSHS rounds across five countries, girls who use a mobile phone three or more hours a day report loneliness 8 percentage points higher and suicidal ideation 10 points higher than girls who use a phone less, with rates rising steadily at higher hours. That corresponds to an odds ratio of roughly 1.5 to 1.7, similar to the cross-sectional estimates in U.S. and European surveys.
- In the 2022 Nepal DHS, self-reported PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores among 15–19-year-old women show a positive, though imprecisely estimated, within-cluster association with daily internet use.
- The national U.S. trends line up across sources: NSDUH youth depression turns upward in 2011–12 and YRBS sadness follows, the increases are consistently larger for girls than for boys, and the ACS cognitive-difficulty rate among adults 65 and older falls over the same decade.
- In state-level panels, the NTIA share of teen households using smartphones for internet access predicts YRBS girls' sadness (+0.9 pp per 10 percentage points, SE 0.44), though this relationship does not hold at the county level.

<a id="review-where-the-pilot-finds-no-effect-and-how-to-interpret-the-difference"></a>

### Where the pilot finds no effect, and how to interpret the difference

1.  **LTE rollout at the metro and county levels.** Most of the natural experiments cited in the *Anxious Generation* literature estimate the effect of *first* wired broadband access in the 2000s, or of Facebook first arriving on college campuses. By contrast, 4G LTE in 2011–2013 was a speed upgrade layered onto existing 3G smartphones and mobile Facebook; most large U.S. metros received LTE within a two-year window; and if social media operates partly through peer norms and national platforms, teenagers in later-adopting markets were exposed alongside early-adopting ones. Each of these factors attenuates geographic comparisons across U.S. markets. Finding a null effect for LTE timing therefore indicates that U.S. metro rollout dates cannot isolate the 2010s shift, not that smartphones were harmless.  
      
    The closest geographic parallel that does find an effect in the smartphone era is Elaine Guo's [British Columbia study](http://hdl.handle.net/1807/130332). Guo compares teenagers in rural mountain communities that gained high-speed fixed wireless internet (25 Mbps over cellular infrastructure) with teenagers in mountain communities that remained unserved, comparing girls with boys before and after 2014 using administrative school records on severe mental-health designations (which require a clinical diagnosis). Starting in 2014, girls in covered communities experienced a roughly 1 percentage point increase in severe designations relative to boys—about 90% of their baseline rate—with no corresponding shift for boys, moderate designations, or unrelated disabilities. Three features distinguish Guo's setting from our U.S. LTE panel: the treatment is a transition from little or no home broadband to high-speed access in isolated towns rather than a 3G-to-4G upgrade in metropolitan areas; the outcome is a clinical school designation rather than a census disability screener; and the time contrast compares pre- and post-2014 periods against a 2019 coverage map rather than staggered rollout dates (which is also a limitation of that study, since earlier annual coverage maps were unavailable). Taken together, the two analyses suggest that geographic designs can detect a 2010s connectivity effect only where broadband access itself was newly introduced and where the outcome captures clinical internalizing disorders.
2.  **Country-level GSHS panels with national internet, mobile-broadband, and 3G/4G series.** Regressing country-round survey means on national ITU penetration series is subject to the same aggregation problems that Haidt and coauthors [highlight](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/21677026261425910) in Vuorre and Przybylski's 72-country Facebook study: national averages pool adult and youth access and move with broader economic trends. Our country-level GSHS regressions should be read with the same caution.
3.  **Caregiver reports in 67 MICS surveys.** The MICS analysis provides a more substantive null result. Across 507,478 children in low- and middle-income countries, caregiver-reported anxiety and depression among 10–17-year-olds show no meaningful relationship with local young-adult internet use or with a teenage girl's own daily phone or internet use within the same sampling cluster; the small positive cluster correlation for girls' anxiety is mirrored among 5–9-year-olds who do not use phones. Two interpretations remain open: either the self-report correlations in school surveys partly reflect reverse causation and shared reporting style (distressed adolescents both use phones more and report more symptoms), or caregivers frequently miss internalizing symptoms in their children (consistent with clinical evidence that parent–child agreement on internalizing disorders is low). Public cross-sections cannot separate these two explanations, which motivates linking adolescent self-reports to external data on local network rollout.

<a id="review-two-empirical-patterns-the-existing-debate-has-largely-overlooked"></a>

### Two empirical patterns the existing debate has largely overlooked

- Perceived schoolwork pressure rose after 2010 across roughly 45 HBSC countries, not only in the United States, and psychosomatic complaints rose more in countries where pressure increased more. Although the within-country slope is modest and matches the pre-2010 baseline relationship, the post-2010 rise in perceived academic pressure is a broad cross-national trend that dismissals based on single-country exam reforms do not address.
- In U.S. state youth surveys with post-2021 waves, adolescent sadness and suicidal ideation have fallen substantially from their 2021 peaks—in Washington, 2025 sadness is below its 2010 rate—without a corresponding drop in daily smartphone or social-media use. Neither a simple screen-dose account nor a simple academic-pressure account explains that downturn without additional mechanisms, such as changes in school phone restrictions or shifts in platform content.

**Summary.** Prior literature documents a consistent individual-level correlation between heavy screen use and adolescent distress alongside causal effects from earlier broadband and Facebook rollouts, while Guo's British Columbia study extends that causal evidence to rural wireless access and clinical diagnoses after 2014. Our pilot reproduces the individual-level association in developing-country school surveys, but finds that U.S. 4G rollout dates, county adoption rates, and caregiver reports in 67 MICS surveys show no corresponding effect. Resolving whether the self-reported association is causal requires pairing adolescent-reported symptoms and phone use with exogenous local variation—most promisingly, the staggered 2024–26 U.S. school phone bans and subnational mobile-coverage rollouts.

<a id="review-next"></a>

## Conclusions and next steps

Combining public microdata across the United States and more than 80 other countries narrows the debate in several ways while leaving the core causal question open.

| Hypothesis                   | Where it stands after the pilot                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| H1 · Phones and social media | The cross-sectional individual association is robust and extends to developing countries: teenage girls who use mobile phones heavily report substantially higher loneliness and suicidal ideation in Ghana, India, Jamaica, Morocco, and Nepal just as in Western surveys, with the same sex asymmetry and dose-response gradient. Yet every test based on rollout timing or adult- and cluster-measured exposure is null: 4G launch dates across U.S. metros and counties, metro adoption rates in the county panels, cluster connectivity and own use in 67 MICS caregiver surveys, and national 3G/4G coverage in 34 GSHS countries. Either the causal effect operates through peer norms and national platforms too uniformly for subnational timing designs to detect, or the individual correlation largely reflects reverse causation and shared vulnerabilities. School phone bans in PISA 2022 and Norway provide modest evidence of a girl-specific benefit. |
| H2 · School pressure         | The descriptive premise of Gray's account holds up better than critics often acknowledge: perceived schoolwork pressure rose after 2010 across most HBSC countries, and U.S. weekday homework time rose by roughly 40%. However, perceived pressure behaves like a steady correlate of psychosomatic complaints (with the same within-country slope before and after 2010) rather than the driver of the post-2010 break; U.S. state accountability reforms show no effect; and the ACS age gradient does not peak in the high-stakes high-school years. A key constraint is measurement: public U.S. surveys lack longitudinal school-level pressure items, making H2 harder to test subnationally than H1.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| H3 · Interaction             | State accountability policies interacted with metro 4G launch dates show no positive effect on the ACS item, but the school-day version of the interaction hypothesis—smartphones operating inside high-pressure school hours—is consistent with the school-ban evidence: bans reduce daily in-school phone use and classroom distraction, girls in ban schools report lower loneliness and device anxiety, the loneliness reduction is directionally larger among students with high mathematics anxiety, Norway's middle-school bans reduced girls' psychological consultations, and U.S. adolescent sadness moved inversely to national school phone restrictions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| H0 · Measurement             | Ruled out as the primary explanation: the post-2010 rise appears simultaneously across diagnostic interviews, self-report school surveys, and the ACS cognitive-difficulty item; the 65+ comparison group trends downward over the same decade; and the increase is consistently concentrated among girls. Differential awareness and diagnosis-seeking likely contribute to the steeper relative rise among affluent and private-school teens, but do not account for the overall trend.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

Three empirical findings from the pilot stand out beyond the existing book-length arguments. First, the 2010s rise in adolescent distress occurred almost simultaneously across U.S. states and counties with very different mobile-rollout and school-policy timelines, which explains why coarse geographic designs struggle to separate the competing hypotheses and why national time series can be cited in support of either view. Second, post-2021 waves of the U.S. state youth surveys show a substantial decline in sadness and suicidal ideation—returning to or below 2010 levels in Washington and Illinois—without a matching drop in daily phone or social-media use, coinciding instead with the re-tightening of school phone rules. Any purely dose-based account of screen time or school pressure has to account for that downturn. Third, across developing-country surveys, the link between phone use and distress appears consistently when adolescents report both their own hours and their own symptoms (GSHS, Nepal DHS), but vanishes when symptoms are reported by caregivers (67 MICS surveys). Resolving why self-reports and caregiver reports diverge is central to the next phase of work.

**Priority next steps for Phase 2.**

- Track the 2023–27 U.S. state and district school phone bans through the 2025–27 YRBS and county youth survey waves, separately by sex and across at least two post-ban years, retaining the 65+ comparison group. The 51-state policy table and panel code are in place; the 2025 YRBS state files will provide the first post-ban wave.
- License GSMA mobile-coverage polygons and request MICS and DHS cluster coordinates to test adolescent-reported phone use and mental health (GSHS 2022–23, incoming MICS7 rounds, and DHS-8 mental-health modules) against local network rollout timing.
- Request the student-level HBSC microdata to test whether psychosomatic complaints became more concentrated among high-pressure students after 2010 and to estimate the student-level interaction between problematic social-media use, schoolwork pressure, and school phone rules.
- Further extensions of the ACS market event study or the IPUMS International census cognitive-difficulty item are unlikely to add much; both measures are too coarse for a geographic timing design. Federal Statistical Research Data Center (FSRDC) applications for restricted NSDUH or NHANES geocodes should wait until the state-survey or phone-ban evaluations establish a clearer subnational signal.

Reproducibility: analysis scripts are in `scripts/` and output tables are in `results/tables/` of the project repository. Data sources: IPUMS USA (ACS 1-year 2005–2024), IPUMS ATUS 2003–2024, IPUMS MICS (68 surveys), IPUMS International (Kenya 2009/2019, Mexico 2010/2020), Census CPS Computer and Internet Use Supplements (2009–2023), OECD PISA 2022, WHO GSHS (165 country-rounds), WHO HBSC, DHS-8 (Nepal 2022, Kenya 2022), and public NSDUH, NHANES, YRBS, NCES SSOCS/School Pulse, and state youth survey files as documented in each section.
